title: The Ship of State
text:
In Book VI of Plato's Republic, Socrates explains why the best qualified people are rarely the ones in charge of a city. He uses an image of a ship.

The owner of the ship is bigger and stronger than anyone on board, but he is a little deaf, somewhat short-sighted, and knows little about sailing. The sailors quarrel with each other over who should steer. None of them has ever learned navigation, and they insist it cannot even be taught, and they are ready to tear to pieces anyone who says it can. They crowd around the owner, begging him to hand them the helm. When others win his favor, they kill them or throw them overboard. Then they drug or intoxicate the owner, take control of the ship, help themselves to the cargo, and sail along drinking and feasting.

They praise as a fine navigator anyone who helps them get control, and call anyone who does not useless. They have no idea that a true navigator must study the seasons, the sky, the stars and the winds. If such a person were on board, they would call him a stargazer and a babbler, good for nothing.

Socrates' point is that philosophers are scorned in cities for the same reason: the people who should steer are dismissed by those who only know how to win the owner's favor.
lesson: Being good at getting the job and being good at doing it are different skills. When you choose who steers, weigh real expertise over charm, loyalty and noise.
people: Socrates, Adeimantus, the shipowner, the sailors, the true navigator
